items.stem: What is the name for "a layer of thin, flat cells forming the walls of alveoli and capillaries"?
items.answer: Squamous epithelium

items.stem: Explain why the trachea is supported by C-shaped rings of cartilage rather than complete rings.
items.answer: Cartilage prevents collapse when pressure falls during inspiration; the gap allows the oesophagus to expand when food is swallowed and lets the trachea flex.
items.markingKey: Cartilage prevents collapse when pressure falls during inspiration [1]; the gap allows the oesophagus to expand when food is swallowed and lets the trachea flex [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the distribution of cartilage, smooth muscle and elastic fibres changes from trachea to alveoli.
items.answer: Cartilage decreases (rings → plates → none); smooth muscle present to bronchioles, absent in alveoli; elastic fibres throughout.
items.markingKey: Cartilage decreases (rings → plates → none) [1]; smooth muscle present to bronchioles, absent in alveoli [1]; elastic fibres throughout [1] [3]

items.stem: Leila, a student in Kathmandu, examined prepared slides of transverse sections of the trachea, a bronchiole and alveolar tissue with a light microscope. items.answer: (a) Trachea has C-shaped cartilage rings and many goblet cells; bronchiole has no cartilage, more smooth muscle relative to size, few goblet cells. (b) 250 μm

items.stem: Explain why an asthma attack makes breathing difficult.
items.answer: Smooth muscle in bronchioles contracts and the lining becomes inflamed with extra mucus, narrowing the airways and increasing resistance to air flow.

items.stem: Explain how ventilation and blood flow maintain a steep concentration gradient.
items.answer: Breathing brings fresh air high in O₂ and removes CO₂; blood flow carries O₂ away and brings CO₂, so the gradients are maintained.

items.stem: At rest, Mohammed has a tidal volume of 0.55 dm³ and a breathing rate of 15 breaths min⁻¹. During exercise these become 3.0 dm³ and 35 breaths min⁻¹. (a) Calculate the ventilation rate at rest and during exercise. (b) Calculate the percentage increase.
items.answer: (a) rest 8.25 dm³ min⁻¹; exercise 105 dm³ min⁻¹ (b) 1173%

items.stem: At rest, Isla has a tidal volume of 0.4 dm³ and a breathing rate of 12 breaths min⁻¹. During exercise these become 1.5 dm³ and 45 breaths min⁻¹. (a) Calculate the ventilation rate at rest and during exercise. (b) Calculate the percentage increase. (c) Explain why ventilation increases during exercise.
items.answer: (a) rest 4.8 dm³ min⁻¹; exercise 67.5 dm³ min⁻¹ (b) 1306% (c) Muscles respire faster, producing more CO₂ and using more O₂; increased ventilation maintains steep concentration gradients at the alveoli so more O₂ diffuses in and CO₂ out.

items.stem: A mountaineer climbs to 5,500 m in the Himalayas, where the partial pressure of oxygen in the air is about 10.6 kPa compared with 21 kPa at sea level. (a) Explain why less oxygen diffuses into the blood at this altitude. (b) Suggest two ways in which the body adjusts after several weeks at altitude.
items.answer: (a) Lower pO₂ in alveoli gives a smaller concentration gradient between air and blood, so the rate of diffusion falls. (b) More red blood cells / haemoglobin; deeper and faster breathing; more capillaries; more myoglobin / mitochondria.

items.answer: Dust; pollen; bacteria; viruses; spores.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Dust; pollen; bacteria; viruses; spores (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: A student in Mumbai states: "Cilia trap pathogens." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Mucus traps pathogens; cilia move the mucus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Mucus traps pathogens; cilia move the mucus. [2]

items.stem: Lina says: "Goblet cells are found in the alveoli." Explain whether Lina is correct.
items.answer: Goblet cells are in the trachea, bronchi and larger bronchioles, not alveoli.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Goblet cells are in the trachea, bronchi and larger bronchioles, not alveoli. [2]

items.stem: In a healthy person in Doha, mucus moves up the trachea at 10 mm min⁻¹. In a long-term smoker the rate is 3.2 mm min⁻¹. The trachea is 15 cm long. (a) Calculate the time taken for mucus to travel the length of the trachea in each person. (b) Explain the difference and suggest one consequence for the smoker.
items.answer: (a) healthy 15 min; smoker 46.9 min (b) Smoke paralyses / destroys cilia (and increases mucus), so mucus moves more slowly; pathogens remain longer in the airways, increasing infections (bronchitis) and coughing.

items.stem: Describe how the airways are protected by ciliated epithelium, goblet cells and mucus, and explain how smoking affects this protection.
items.answer: Goblet cells and glands secrete mucus (mucins) that traps dust and pathogens; cilia beat in coordinated waves moving mucus up to the throat (mucus escalator); swallowed. Smoking: tar paralyses / destroys cilia, more goblet cells, mucus accumulates, infection, bronchitis, coughing.
items.markingKey: mucus [1]; goblet cells [1]; cilia / escalator [2]; effects of smoking [2] [6]

items.stem: Why is cartilage absent from bronchioles?
options: They are small enough to stay open without it, and this allows their diameter to change
They have elastic fibres instead of epithelium
They are part of the alveoli
items.answer: They are small enough to stay open without it, and this allows their diameter to change
items.markingKey: Smooth muscle changes their diameter.

items.stem: A student in Kathmandu states: "Gas exchange takes place across the walls of the bronchioles." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Gas exchange happens across alveolar walls.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Gas exchange happens across alveolar walls. [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the trachea is supported by C-shaped rings of cartilage rather than complete rings. (b) Explain how the distribution of cartilage, smooth muscle and elastic fibres changes from trachea to alveoli.
items.answer: (a) Cartilage prevents collapse when pressure falls during inspiration; the gap allows the oesophagus to expand when food is swallowed and lets the trachea flex. (b) Cartilage decreases (rings → plates → none); smooth muscle present to bronchioles, absent in alveoli; elastic fibres throughout.
items.markingKey: (a) Cartilage prevents collapse when pressure falls during inspiration [1]; the gap allows the oesophagus to expand when food is swallowed and lets the trachea flex [1] [2] (b) Cartilage decreases (rings → plates → none) [1]; smooth muscle present to bronchioles, absent in alveoli [1]; elastic fibres throughout [1] [3]

items.stem: Tomás measures the image of a ciliated epithelial cell in a micrograph as 48 mm. The magnification is ×1,000. Calculate the actual length of a ciliated epithelial cell, giving your answer in micrometres (μm).

A student in Bogotá examined a section of lung tissue and recorded: ciliated epithelium: present (in larger bronchioles); smooth muscle: present; elastic fibres: present. Identify the region of the gas exchange system and give two reasons.
items.answer: Bronchiole: ciliated epithelium present (in larger bronchioles); smooth muscle present.
items.markingKey: bronchiole [1]; two reasons from the observations [2] [3]

items.stem: A student in Accra examined a section of lung tissue and recorded: elastic fibres: present; ciliated epithelium: present; smooth muscle: present. Identify the region of the gas exchange system and give two reasons.
items.answer: Bronchus: elastic fibres present; ciliated epithelium present.
items.markingKey: bronchus [1]; two reasons from the observations [2] [3]

items.stem: Daniel, a student in Seoul, examined prepared slides of transverse sections of the trachea, a bronchiole and alveolar tissue with a light microscope. (a) Explain how the structure of the alveolar wall is related to its function. (b) Suggest why the slides are stained.
items.answer: (a) Squamous epithelium one cell thick – short diffusion distance; elastic fibres for recoil; close contact with capillaries. (b) To increase contrast so different tissues / cells are distinguished.
items.markingKey: (a) Squamous epithelium one cell thick – short diffusion distance [1]; elastic fibres for recoil [1]; close contact with capillaries [1] [3] (b) To increase contrast so different tissues / cells are distinguished [1]

items.stem: Mei, a student in Auckland, examined prepared slides of transverse sections of the trachea, a bronchiole and alveolar tissue with a light microscope. (a) Describe two differences you would expect between the trachea and a bronchiole. (b) Explain how the structure of the alveolar wall is related to its function. (c) Suggest why the slides are stained.
items.answer: (a) Trachea has C-shaped cartilage rings and many goblet cells; bronchiole has no cartilage, more smooth muscle relative to size, few goblet cells. (b) Squamous epithelium one cell thick – short diffusion distance; elastic fibres for recoil; close contact with capillaries. (c) To increase contrast so different tissues / cells are distinguished.

items.stem: State why red blood cells are squeezed against capillary walls in the lungs.
items.answer: The capillary lumen is narrow, so the diffusion distance is shorter and the cells move slowly.
items.markingKey: The capillary lumen is narrow, so the diffusion distance is shorter and the cells move slowly [1]

items.stem: A patient with fibrosis has thickened alveolar walls. The diffusion distance is tripled while the surface area and concentration difference stay the same. State and explain how the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood changes.
items.answer: The rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood becomes one third.
items.markingKey: Using Fick's law: rate ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ diffusion distance: rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood ∝ diffusion distance^−1.00; factor = 3.00^−1.00 = 0.333. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A student in Madrid states: "Oxygen is actively transported into the blood in the lungs." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Oxygen diffuses passively down its concentration gradient.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Oxygen diffuses passively down its concentration gradient. [2]

items.stem: A study in Karachi compared healthy lungs with lungs affected by emphysema. Healthy: alveolar surface area 60 m², diffusion distance 0.5 μm. Affected: surface area 19 m², diffusion distance 1.2 μm. Using Fick's law, estimate the rate of diffusion in the affected lung as a fraction of the healthy rate (assume the same concentration difference).

At rest, Omar has a tidal volume of 0.55 dm³ and a breathing rate of 16 breaths min⁻¹. During exercise these become 2.0 dm³ and 35 breaths min⁻¹. (a) Calculate the ventilation rate at rest and during exercise. (b) Calculate the percentage increase.
items.answer: (a) rest 8.8 dm³ min⁻¹; exercise 70 dm³ min⁻¹ (b) 695%

items.stem: A study in Mexico City compared healthy lungs with lungs affected by pulmonary fibrosis. Healthy: alveolar surface area 60 m², diffusion distance 0.5 μm. Affected: surface area 29 m², diffusion distance 1.4 μm. (a) Using Fick's law, estimate the rate of diffusion in the affected lung as a fraction of the healthy rate (assume the same concentration difference). (b) Describe how the structure of healthy alveoli is adapted for gas exchange. (c) Suggest a cause of pulmonary fibrosis.
items.answer: (a) 0.173 (about 17%) (b) Large surface area; walls one cell thick; capillary network; elastic fibres; surfactant; moist. (c) Inhaling dust / fibres (e.g. asbestos), or scarring after infection.

items.stem: A mountaineer climbs to 5,000 m in the Himalayas, where the partial pressure of oxygen in the air is about 11.2 kPa compared with 21 kPa at sea level. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in the partial pressure of oxygen. (b) Explain why less oxygen diffuses into the blood at this altitude. (c) Explain why haemoglobin is less saturated with oxygen at high altitude.
items.answer: (a) 46.7% (b) Lower pO₂ in alveoli gives a smaller concentration gradient between air and blood, so the rate of diffusion falls. (c) At lower pO₂, haemoglobin is lower on the dissociation curve (lower saturation).

items.stem: A patient in Riyadh has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 10 years and now has chronic bronchitis. (a) Explain how smoking leads to chronic bronchitis. (b) Suggest why the patient is at greater risk of lung infections. (c) Explain why the patient becomes short of breath.
items.answer: (a) Tar paralyses / destroys cilia; goblet cells and mucous glands enlarge and produce more mucus; mucus accumulates and bacteria multiply; inflammation; airways narrow; persistent cough. (b) Pathogens trapped in mucus are not removed and can multiply. (c) Mucus and inflammation narrow the airways, so less air reaches alveoli; reduced ventilation and gas exchange.
